summary: Describes a simple TCP transfer protocol for the Internet Registry Information Service. Data moves between client and server in chunks, which enables pipelining. It is on the standards track.

eli5.summary: Sending lookups in small pieces over one connection so many requests can ride along together.

questions: what port does iris xpc use
what is xml pipelining with chunks
how does xpcs work over tls
subtitle: A simple framing for sending IRIS registry queries over TCP, in chunks that can be processed before the whole message arrives.

tldr.problem: IRIS, a protocol for looking up registry data, needed a simple transfer protocol over TCP that lets XML be acted on before the entire document has arrived.
tldr.mechanism: XPC wraps XML in blocks made of chunks. A one-octet header and a one-octet chunk descriptor carry flags for keeping the session open, the last chunk, and the chunk type.
tldr.outcome: It became the default transport for IRIS, replacing the BEEP mapping in that role, and it is updated by RFC 8996.

today: RFC 4992 is a Proposed Standard that updates RFC 3981 and is itself updated by RFC 8996. It has not been obsoleted.

sections.title: Introduction and Session Lifecycle
sections.content:
The Internet Registry Information Service (IRIS) can use several transfer protocols, chosen by the server operator and discovered with S-NAPTR. XML pipelining with chunks (XPC) is a TCP transfer protocol that any IRIS registry type can use. Its use with IRIS is called IRIS-XPC.

XPC defines simple framing so that XML fragments can be acted on (pipelined) before the whole XML instance has been received. It is meant for plain request and response exchanges. The client sends requests in data blocks, and the server answers each block with a corresponding block on the same connection.

A session runs through these phases: the client opens a TCP connection, the server sends a connection response block, the client sends a request block, the server sends a response block, and the pair repeats while the session stays open. Then the TCP connection is closed.
sections.eli5: You call a shop. The shop answers first, you ask your question, the shop replies, and you can ask again until one of you hangs up.

sections.title: Request and Response Blocks
sections.content:
A request block (RQB) holds a one-octet header, a one-octet authority length, an authority of 0 to 255 octets, and one or more chunks. The authority names the registry authority the request is meant for, and its length MUST match the length field exactly.

A response block (RSB) is simpler: a header followed by chunks. Servers SHOULD NOT send an RSB until they have received the whole RQB. A server that starts early must remember that the client will not process the response until it has finished sending, and that the response may fill the client's TCP buffers.

A connection response block (CRB) is an RSB the server sends as soon as a connection opens. It has exactly one chunk. Either it carries version information with the keep-open flag set to 1, which tells the client the service is available, or it carries a system-error with the flag set to 0, after which the server closes the connection. Servers MUST use the second form when they can accept connections but cannot process requests.
sections.eli5: The first thing the shop says tells you if it is open. After that, your question comes with the name of who you want to talk to, and the answer comes back as a simple reply.

sections.title: Block Header and Chunk Descriptor
sections.content:
Every block starts with a one-octet block header. Bits 0 and 1 are the version; zero means the protocol in this document. Bit 2 is the keep-open (KO) flag. In a request, 1 asks the server not to close the TCP session, and 0 means the client expects the server to close right after replying. In a response, 1 means the server expects the client to keep the session open, and 0 means the client should close right after this block. Bits 3 to 7 are reserved and MUST be 0.

Each chunk begins with a one-octet chunk descriptor, followed by a two-octet chunk data length and the data. In the descriptor, bit 0 is the last-chunk (LC) flag and bit 1 is the data-complete (DC) flag, which says the chunk ends the data for its type. Bits 2 to 4 are reserved and MUST be 0, and bits 5 to 7 give the chunk type.

A block MAY contain several chunk types, but chunks of one type MUST be contiguous and in the order their data is to be read. The type groups appear in this order: authentication chunks, then data chunks, then information chunks. A block MUST contain at least one chunk.
sections.eli5: Each package has a small sticker on it. One sticker says whether to keep talking afterwards, and another says whether this is the last piece and what kind of piece it is.

sections.title: Chunk Types
sections.content:
The three-bit chunk type has eight values. Application data (ad, 111) carries the IRIS XML itself. Version information (vi, 001) carries a <versions> document; the transfer protocol identifier for this specification is iris.xpc1. A client MAY send a version chunk, which SHOULD be zero length, and the server MUST answer with one, which lets the client ask what a server supports.

Size information (si) and other information (oi) chunks are sent by servers; clients MUST NOT send them. Other information carries an error type such as block-error, data-error, system-error, authority-error or idle-timeout. A block-error is for malformed blocks, including an incomplete block when the connection has been idle. Two minutes is RECOMMENDED for that timeout.

SASL chunks (sd) carry a mechanism name and mechanism data, and a server that finishes a SASL exchange MUST answer with an authentication success (as) or authentication failure (af) chunk. A no data chunk (nd) is ignored by the receiver.
sections.eli5: Pieces come in different kinds: real questions and answers, version notes, error notes, and password-check notes. A tag on each piece tells the reader which kind it is.

sections.title: Idle Sessions and Errors
sections.content:
A server that needs to close an idle connection SHOULD first send an unsolicited response block with an idle-timeout error and the KO flag set to 0, then close the TCP connection.

A server closing because of an error SHOULD send a response block with a block-error, a data-error or version information, again with KO set to 0, and then close the TCP connection. This is also the behavior for an unsupported version or for reserved bits that the server does not understand.
sections.eli5: If nobody speaks for a long time, or something goes wrong, the shop says so politely and then hangs up.

sections.title: TLS and SASL Security
sections.content:
XPC can run inside TLS, started right after the TCP session opens and before any block is sent. This is called XPCS. Server authentication follows the convention used by IRIS-BEEP. XPC and XPCS have separate URI schemes (iris.xpc and iris.xpcs) and S-NAPTR labels, but both use the same iris.xpc1 value in version information.

Clients SHOULD be prepared to use SASL/DIGEST-MD5 or SASL/OTP for user authentication, and TLS with a list of RSA cipher suites using 3DES, AES-128 or AES-256, with or without client certificates. Anonymous access SHOULD be considered either by using no authentication or by using SASL/ANONYMOUS. Clients MUST NOT use SASL/PLAIN without first encrypting the session, and MUST implement SASL/PLAIN with TLS using the TLS_RSA_WITH_3DES_EDE_CBC_SHA cipher.

The SASL service name is iris-xpc. When TLS and SASL are combined, TLS MUST be applied first. Multiple SASL authentications are not supported, and an endpoint that wants to abort an authentication exchange MUST close the connection.
sections.eli5: For secret things, you can lock the phone line first and then show your ID. Passwords must never be spoken on an unlocked line.

sections.title: Registrations and the Default Transport
sections.content:
This RFC updates RFC 3981, which had named IRIS-BEEP as the default transport for IRIS. IRIS-XPC becomes the default transport instead.

IANA registrations cover the iris.xpc and iris.xpcs URI schemes, matching S-NAPTR application protocol labels, and two well-known TCP ports: 713 for XPC and 714 for XPCS. Neither uses broadcast or multicast. XML in these chunks MUST use only UTF-8 or UTF-16.
sections.eli5: Two phone numbers were set aside for this service, one for the plain line and one for the locked line.

messages.label: CRB
messages.note: Version information; KO is 1, so the service is available.

messages.label: RQB
messages.note: Authority plus request chunks; may ask to keep the session open.

messages.label: RSB
messages.note: Response chunks; says whether the session will close.

fields.name: Version (V)
fields.desc: Zero means the version defined in this document.

fields.name: Keep Open (KO)
fields.desc: Asks for, or announces, an open session.

fields.name: Last Chunk (LC)
fields.desc: 1 means the last chunk in the block.

fields.name: Data Complete (DC)
fields.desc: 1 means the end of the data for this chunk type.

fields.name: Chunk Type (CT)
fields.desc: Kind of data in the chunk.

items.label: nd
items.desc: No data; ignored by the receiver.
